title: Leviathan, King over All the Proud
summary: God's second speech reaches its climax with Leviathan, a creature of the sea that no hook can catch and no weapon can wound. God asks whether Job can tame it, make a covenant with it, or sell it in the market, and then describes its scales, its fiery breath, its iron-hard chest, and the churning wake it leaves in the deep. Nothing on earth is its equal; it is king over all the proud, and yet it is God's creature.
story: This is the last and longest portrait in God's speeches. Chapter 40 described Behemoth, the great beast of the marsh; now God turns to Leviathan, the monster of the waters. The name is not new to the book. In chapter 3, cursing the day of his birth, Job called on those who are ready to rouse Leviathan (3:8), and here God declares that no one is so fierce as to rouse him. Job had invoked chaos against his own life; God shows that even the embodiment of chaos is his creature. When the speech ends, Job will answer for the last time in chapter 42, and the book will turn to its prose conclusion.
historical:
Leviathan appears in several places in the Old Testament, and the texts suggest two overlapping pictures. In Psalm 104:26 Leviathan is a sea creature God formed to play in the sea. In Psalm 74:13-14 and Isaiah 27:1 Leviathan is a many-headed serpent or dragon of the sea whom God crushes, a symbol of chaos and of hostile powers. The same figure appears in Canaanite poetry from Ugarit (before 1200 BC) as Litan, a twisting, seven-headed sea serpent defeated by the storm god Baal or his sister Anat. Some of the descriptive phrases Isaiah uses for Leviathan closely match the Ugaritic ones.

Many scholars think the portrait in Job 41 draws on the Nile crocodile, whose armored scales, fearsome teeth, and resistance to weapons fit much of the description. Crocodiles were familiar in Egypt, where they were feared and even worshiped in connection with the god Sobek. Others think the fiery breath and smoking nostrils (verses 18 to 21) point beyond any real animal to the mythic dragon. A common view combines the two: the poet describes a creature like the crocodile in the heightened language of the chaos monster, so that the most terrifying thing in nature and in the imagination stands before God as his creature.
cultural:
Verses 1 to 8 pile up images from everyday life in order to make them absurd. Fishermen landed fish with hooks and ropes and kept live catches on cords through the gills or jaw. Captives and slaves were sometimes led by a rope or ring through the nose, a practice Assyrian reliefs depict. A covenant could bind a servant to a master for life (compare Exodus 21:5-6). Children kept birds as pets, merchants bartered goods, and traders divided a catch among themselves. God asks whether Leviathan can be treated in any of these ways, and the answer is obviously no.

The word for traders or merchants in verse 6 is the same as the word for Canaanites, whose name had become a byword for merchants because of the famous trading cities of the Phoenician coast. The description of the sea churned into foam like ointment boiling in a pot, and the wake like white hair on the deep, would have been vivid to anyone who had seen a large animal thrashing in water.
literary: The chapter is a single sustained poem. Verses 1 to 11 are a series of taunting questions: can you catch him, tame him, sell him, fight him? Verse 10 draws the conclusion: if no one dares to rouse Leviathan, who can stand against God himself? Verse 11 then states the principle that no one has a claim on God. Verses 12 to 34 describe Leviathan from head to tail, moving from his jaws and scales to his fiery breath, his neck and chest, his invulnerability to weapons, his underside, and finally his wake through the deep. The description ends with the verdict that he is king over all the proud, a deliberate link back to 40:11-12, where God challenged Job to humble every proud man.

outline.t: Can you catch, tame, or sell Leviathan?
If no one can face him, who can face God?
His jaws and his armor of scales
Fire, smoke, and an iron-hard frame
His wake through the deep and his rule over the proud

doctrines.note: Leviathan, the most fearsome creature imaginable, is God's handiwork. If no one can stand before Leviathan, no one can stand before God. God rules over even the forces that humans experience as chaos.
God speaks of Leviathan with evident delight: he cannot keep silent about its limbs, its power, and its graceful form. Even the most dangerous creature is part of a creation God made and admires.
Everything under heaven belongs to God, and no one has first given to him that he should repay. God is free and owes nothing to any creature, which means every good gift from him is grace.

words.note: Livyatan, Leviathan, probably from a root meaning to twist or coil. The name fits a serpent or a thrashing sea creature. In the Old Testament it names both a real sea creature (Psalm 104:26) and the mythic chaos monster God defeats (Isaiah 27:1). Job 41 plays on both.

Berit, covenant, the Bible's great word for binding relationship, used of God's covenants with Noah, Abraham, Israel, and David. In verse 4 God asks whether Leviathan will make a covenant with Job to serve him. The irony is sharp: Leviathan will make no covenant with humans, yet God is the one who binds himself by covenant to his people.

Shachats, pride, found only here and in Job 28:8, where it describes proud beasts. The last line of the chapter calls Leviathan king over all the sons of pride. God, who alone can humble the proud (40:11-12), is master even of the creature that rules over them.

Tehom, the deep, the same word used for the watery deep in Genesis 1:2. Leviathan churns it into foam. Because tehom is associated with the primal waters that God ordered at creation, its appearance here reinforces the link between Leviathan and the forces of chaos God governs.

christ: Paul quotes verse 11 near the end of his long argument about God's mercy in Romans: “Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?” (Romans 11:35). For Paul, the line means that salvation cannot be earned; God owes no one, and everything he gives is grace. That use shows how the New Testament read Job's speeches: not as a display of arbitrary power but as the ground of mercy. The Leviathan imagery also feeds into the Bible's larger story of God's victory over chaos and evil. Isaiah promised that the LORD would slay Leviathan the fleeing serpent (Isaiah 27:1), and Revelation pictures the ancient serpent, the dragon, finally overthrown (Revelation 12:9, 20:2). Job 41 itself describes a creature, not Satan, and the link is thematic. But the Christian story says that the power no human could master has been defeated by Christ.

hard.q: Is Leviathan a real animal like the crocodile, or a mythical monster?
hard.a:
Readers have argued for both. Those who favor a real animal point out that the whole speech so far has described real creatures, from lions and ravens to the war horse and Behemoth, and that the crocodile fits the scales, teeth, and resistance to weapons remarkably well. They read the fiery breath as poetic exaggeration, perhaps inspired by the spray a crocodile blows from its nostrils in sunlight. Those who favor a mythic creature point to the other Old Testament passages where Leviathan is a many-headed sea serpent, and to the Ugaritic parallels, and argue that no ordinary animal breathes fire.

Many scholars take a middle path: the poet describes an animal like the crocodile but in the language of the chaos dragon, so that one creature stands for everything in the world that humans fear and cannot master. Whatever Leviathan is, the chapter's point is the same. It is a creature, God made it, and God delights in it. The thing Job cannot face is under God's hand.

questions: Job once called on those who could rouse Leviathan to curse his birth. God now says no one can rouse him. What does that suggest about the limits of human despair before God's rule?
God delights in Leviathan's power and form. What does it mean that God can find beauty even in what frightens us?
Paul used verse 11 to show that everything God gives is grace. How does believing that God owes you nothing change the way you receive what he gives?
